> **Draft.** This document is a first pass at explaining, to a human reader,
> the exact algorithm used by `solve_opening()` in this repository. It is
> written "from the doubts": every section starts from a real question that
> was asked while reading the code, and each question is the door to a
> formal concept. Sections will be deepened one by one.

# A question from the game table

You draw your 14 tiles in Rummikub. To "open", you must lay on the table one
or more melds whose total is **at least 30 points** — and you may touch no
tile that is already on the board.

Natural questions:

1. **How often** can a random hand of 14 tiles open on its first turn?
2. If it cannot, **how many draws** do you need on average before it can?

The answer to (1) is **about 49.5%** of hands, and (2) is **about 2.4 draws**
(we will come back to these numbers in [Honest science](#honest-science)).

But notice what the machine must do to answer (1): for *each* simulated hand
it must decide exactly whether a 30-point opening exists. "Exactly" is the
hard part. A hand of 14 tiles can form hundreds of candidate melds, and melds
share tiles, so "try all combinations" is not obviously fast.

::: {.callout-note}
**Concept box — optimization**
Deciding *does an opening exist?* is an optimization problem: find the
maximum total score achievable with a valid set of melds, and compare it to
30. The algorithm that solves it exactly — in milliseconds — is the topic of
this text: **branch & bound**.
:::

# The mathematical problem under the hood

What does it mean that the melds are *disjoint*? Simply that you cannot play
the same physical tile twice: if a meld uses the tile `4blue`, no other meld
in your opening may use it. Melds that share no tile are called
**disjoint**.

This little word is the heart of the problem. Think of each meld as a
*set* of tiles. We must choose a collection of sets that:

- do not **overlap** (the disjoint condition), and
- **maximize** the sum of their values.

This is a well-known combinatorial problem:

::: {.callout-important}
**Formal concept — weighted set packing**
Choosing non-overlapping sets to maximize the total value is **weighted set
packing** — a problem with deep roots in combinatorial optimization. It is
equivalent to an **integer program (0-1)**: one binary variable per candidate
meld, a constraint *sum ≤ 1* for every tile (each tile can belong to at most
one chosen meld), and an objective of maximizing the weighted sum
[@barnhart1998]. Set packing is one of the original NP-complete problems
identified by Karp in 1972 [@karp1972], and its many relatives are catalogued
in the standard reference on intractability [@garey1979]. So in the worst
case any exact algorithm can take exponential time — and even *approximating*
it is hard: it cannot be approximated within a factor of Ω(k/log k) unless
P = NP [@hazan2006], where k is the largest size of a set.
:::

Why does this matter to you as a player? Because it tells you *why* there is
no obvious shortcut. The hardness is not just theoretical: the most natural
greedy idea — always take the most valuable meld that still fits — has a
worst-case guarantee that grows with k, the size of the largest meld
[@chandra2001]. Rummikub melds are small (a group has at most 4 tiles, a run
at most 13), yet the hand h1 below will show that even at this scale the
greedy can be wrong. And the warning stands: an exact algorithm must be
exponential in the worst case, so the practical trick is to make the
*typical* case fast.

# The idea: search, but search smartly

What is branch & bound, and what are the branches?

Branch & bound answers two questions at once:

- **How do we explore all possibilities without repeating any?**
  (*branching*)
- **How do we skip most of them anyway?** (*bounding* + *pruning*)

Branching builds a **decision tree**. At every node we pick one tile and ask:
*do we discard it, or use it in one of the melds that contains it?* Each
answer is a branch. Every complete path through the tree is a complete
decision about every tile, and the tree visits every possible play exactly
once. The general scheme — *branch*, *bound*, *prune* — is one of the oldest
tools of combinatorial optimization; its first systematic treatment dates
back to Lawler and Wood's survey [@lawler1966].

We will use one hand throughout the text. Call it **h1**:

- `2blue 3blue 4blue 5blue` plus an extra `4blue`, plus `4black 4yellow`.

It can form four melds:

| Meld  | Tiles            | Points |
|-------|------------------|--------|
| M01   | 2 3 4 (blue)     | 9      |
| M02   | 2 3 4 5 (blue)   | 14     |
| M03   | 3 4 5 (blue)     | 12     |
| M04   | 4blue 4yellow 4black | 12 |

Note the conflict: M02 wants *one* `4blue`, but the extra `4blue` is what
M04 needs. Some tile must be sacrificed. The tree below is the machine
exploring that conflict.

![Search tree for h1 with no target (exact maximum). Orange edges highlight
the path of each node that improved the best score; the red `x` is a pruned
branch.](./../results/demo_bnb_example1_max.png)

## The most constrained tile

What is the most constrained tile, and why is it safe to force the choice on
it?

At the root, h1 has six tile types. The algorithm does not pick a random
tile: it picks the one that belongs to the *fewest* usable melds. That is
`4yellow`, which appears only in M04. The question "discard it or use it?"
then splits the problem in two, and **every** possible play falls into one of
the two branches — nothing is lost, so the search stays exact.

::: {.callout-note}
**Formal concept — MRV / fail-first**
Picking the most restricted variable first is the **minimum remaining values
(MRV)** heuristic of constraint satisfaction (CSP), also known as the
**fail-first principle**: a tile that fits in few melds is the one most
likely to close a branch quickly, and failing early costs the least.
:::

The "safe" property is what mathematicians call **completeness**: we only
ever reduce a node to the two cases *use* or *discard*, and those two cases
cover everything.

# The bound: an impossible budget

What exactly does `acc + sum(remaining * values)` do?

Two ingredients:

- `acc` — the score already accumulated along the path from the root to this
  node;
- `remaining` — how many copies of each tile type are still unused;
- `values` — the point value of each tile type.

The quantity `acc + sum(remaining * values)` is a **bound**: the best score
this node could *possibly* reach. Why "possibly"? Because it assumes we can
use **every** remaining tile in a meld, simultaneously — which is usually
impossible, since melds must be disjoint. It is an *optimistic* estimate.

In the h1 trace, the root reports:

```
[N01] remaining: 2bluex1 3bluex1 4bluex2 4yellowx1 4blackx1 5bluex1
      acc= 0  best= 0  BOUND=acc+sum(remaining)=26
```

The five tile types sum to 26, so no play of h1 can ever exceed 26 points.
That single number already tells us something the player can feel at the
table: *h1 cannot open* (26 < 30), before exploring anything.

::: {.callout-important}
**Formal concept — relaxation and admissible heuristics**
Dropping the "disjoint" restriction gives an easier problem whose answer is
an upper bound on the real one. That is exactly the idea behind the
**linear programming relaxation** that powers modern solvers and
**branch-and-price** methods for huge integer programs [@barnhart1998]. A
heuristic that never underestimates is called **admissible**, and it is
exactly the condition that makes the search optimal (the same condition A*
requires for shortest paths).
:::

Because every tile value is non-negative, the bound can only **decrease**
as we go down the tree. We will use that in the next section.

# Pruning: cutting without breaking

What is pruning? And why does it not make the algorithm any less exact?

At any node we know two numbers: the current global best score `best`, and
the node's own optimistic bound. If

```
bound <= best
```

then this node cannot possibly beat the best we already found — even if it
used every remaining tile. We **discard the whole subtree**. In the h1 trace
this happens exactly once, at the very end:

```
[N13] remaining: 5bluex1                   acc=21  best=26  BOUND=acc+sum(remaining)=26
      PRUNE: bound 26 <= best 26 -> this branch cannot improve, discard
```

**Why is it exact?** Because the bound never underestimates: any score
reachable inside the subtree is *at most* the bound, so if the bound cannot
beat `best`, neither can any descendant. Cutting such a subtree loses no
possible improvement. This is a **dominance argument**, and it is the same
logic behind **alpha-beta pruning** in game tree search (there the roles of
`best` are played by alpha/beta).

# How the tree is explored: recursion and backtracking

Why does the 'use 3blue' branch not appear until much later? Where did it go?

Look again at the trace. `3blue` can be used in M03 (`3blue 4blue 5blue`).
You would expect that branch right after the root's "discard `4yellow`"
branch. But in the trace it appears **after** a leaf, like this:

```
[N01] ... BOUND=26
  MOST CONSTRAINED tile: 4yellow
  BRANCH A: discard 4yellow
  [N02] ...
    BRANCH A: discard 2blue
    [N03] ...
      MOST CONSTRAINED tile: 3blue
      BRANCH A: discard 3blue
      [N04] remaining: 4bluex2 4blackx1 5bluex1  acc= 0 ... best=0
        leaf: no meld fits anymore -> best=0
      BRANCH B: use 3blue in meld [12=3blue 4blue 5blue]
      [N05] remaining: 4bluex1 4blackx1        acc=12 ... best=0
        leaf: no meld fits anymore -> best=12
```

The "missing" branch is **N05** — it simply comes *after* the leaf N04, not
before it. The algorithm is **depth-first**: it goes down a branch as far as
it can (to a leaf), then *backtracks* to the last unfinished decision and
tries the other side. The exploration is a stack: enter a node, descend,
return, descend the next option.

::: {.callout-note}
**Formal concept — DFS and backtracking**
This is **depth-first search** over a recursion tree, the classic
**backtracking** pattern: *choose → expand → undo*. The call stack of the
program *is* the memory of the pending decisions. Everything you see in the
console trace `[N01] ... [N13]` is the stack being pushed and popped.
:::

The "bitácora" quality of the trace — the indentation shows the depth, the
`[N..]` number shows the visit order — is precisely what makes the
algorithm teachable: *read the trace in order and you are watching the stack
breathe*.

# The shortcuts: when there is nothing to search

Two special cases are solved with **zero** search:

**Shortcut 1 — you already win.** If any single meld already reaches the
target (≥ 30), you can open with just that meld. Example: the hand
`6..13 blue` has a run of eight tiles worth 76 points, so the machine
answers immediately. The trace prints `done in zero time`.

**Shortcut 2 — you can never win.** If the sum of *all* tile values in the
hand is below the target, even using every tile is not enough. h1 (sum 26)
hits this case with target 30.

These are the **trivial cases** of the problem — they do not change the
worst-case complexity, but they make the *typical* game instant.

# Best-first is not greedy

Here is the subtlest question of all: if the branches are ordered by points,
is the algorithm not just "take the best and done" — a greedy method?

No, and the difference is crucial:

- **Ordering** decides *which* branch to explore first. Branch & bound
  orders the "use" branches by meld value, best first. But it still explores
  *every* non-pruned branch. The ordering is just a preference; it changes
  *speed*, never *correctness*.
- **A greedy method** *decides* permanently: take the best meld, remove its
  tiles, repeat — and never reconsider. It can walk straight into a trap.

Example 3 in the demo shows the trap. The hand is:

```
2blue 3blue 4blue 5blue 6blue  3yellow 3black 4yellow 4black
```

The greedy method (always take the most valuable meld) returns **20
points**. The exact optimum is **24** — a combination the greedy never
considers because its first, locally best choice blocks it.

| Method              | Score |
|---------------------|-------|
| Greedy (best first) | 20    |
| Branch & bound      | 24    |
| Brute force         | 24    |

This is not an anecdote. In the approximation literature, the plain greedy
algorithm for weighted k-set packing is known to be only a k-approximation
in the worst case [@chandra2001]: "take the best and never look back" can
fall arbitrarily far from the optimum, exactly as h3 does.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Lesson.** A *heuristic ordering* inside an exhaustive search is not the
same as a *heuristic decision*. The first only reorders the work; the second
may throw away the optimum. This confusion between "order of exploration"
and "choice" is the most common source of the greedy illusion.
:::

# Honest science: verify, don't trust

How do we *know* the exact search is actually exact? By testing it against
an independent, dumber oracle, and by acknowledging the bugs we find.

**Brute force as oracle.** The demo implements `brute_max()`: it enumerates
every combination of disjoint melds with no pruning and no heuristics —
correct by construction, too slow for large hands. Comparing the two over
random hands:

```
Verified 200 random hands in 1.5s
  branch&bound == brute force in 200/200 cases
  The greedy fell short in 2 of 200 hands (1.0%)
```

**Monte Carlo as statistics.** The opening analysis simulates thousands of
random hands (exactly solved), giving the numbers from the opening of this
text: 49.5% of hands open (95% CI 48.1%–50.8%), 2.40 draws on average.

**And the bug we actually found.** While teaching the algorithm, a regression
test revealed that `possible_melds()` could generate *runs of two tiles*
(12-13 of one colour = 25 points), which are not legal melds. That inflated
the opening statistics (the old 53.5% is wrong). The fix was one guard in
the loop; a regression test now locks it. Two lessons:

- an *algorithmically* correct search is worthless if the *case base*
  (what counts as a meld) is wrong;
- statistics published from a buggy generator are quietly wrong — which is
  why the tests live next to the simulations.

::: {.callout-note}
**Methodological box.** Exact code is not enough; you need (a) an
independent oracle for small instances, (b) statistical sanity checks on
large ones, and (c) regression tests on every bug found. All three are in
this repository.
:::

# Reproduce it

Everything in this text is reproducible from the repository root:

```bash
# The traced algorithm, the greedy trap, the brute-force oracle, the tree
Rscript scripts/demo_branch_and_bound.R

# The opening statistics (Monte Carlo with exact solving)
Rscript scripts/06_opening_analysis.R

# The test suite (including the regression test for the 2-tile run bug)
Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_objective_06.R')"
```

The figures in this document are generated by the demo script and written to
`results/` (a directory of generated outputs, not tracked in git).
